title: What the homepage has to prove for an independent school
metaTitle: What an independent school homepage proves
excerpt: Show students in the school day and a way to visit or inquire. A mission line in small type under a crest does not help a parent choose.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper, the start of a plain sentence rather than a motto in tiny type.
caption: The pen is writing a line someone could read. A homepage should be that readable about the day. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a school homepage show first?
faqs.answer: Students in a real part of the day, and a way to visit or inquire. A parent comparing schools needs to picture a Tuesday and know when they can see it. A crest, a drone of the roof, or an empty chapel does not answer that.

faqs.question: Where should the mission statement go?
faqs.answer: On the about page, in normal type, under a name, if it is true and someone will stand behind it. It should not sit in small type under the hero. If the mission is real, the photograph of the day will already show it.

faqs.question: What facts belong under the first screen?
faqs.answer: Ages, the hours of the day, who is responsible for a class, one honest limit, and a link to fees. Stop before a news grid and a slider of unnamed praise. The heading should name the school and the ages, not say welcome.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An independent school homepage has one job for a parent deciding where a child will spend years. Show students and the day, not a crest, and put a way to visit or inquire on that same first screen. Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay is blunt about the clock: visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear offer in the first 10 seconds is what earns a longer look.

A mission statement in small type does not survive that look. The parent cannot picture a Tuesday from a sentence about excellence. Write the page in this order: the day, the visit, then the few facts that separate your school from the two others on their list. The motto can wait.

## Students in the day, not the emblem

The product is a day in a child's life, repeated for years. A parent who has already accepted your postcode still cannot tell, from a logo, whether their child will be known, bored, hurried, or looked after between lessons. The homepage is where that uncertainty should start to end.

Show one real stretch of the day. Arrival at the gate, a lesson in progress, the break, lunch, the walk to pickup. You do not need all five on the first screen. You need one that is unmistakably your students, in your rooms, in the clothes they actually wear. A child looking at a laptop in a blazer that is not your uniform is a stock photograph. Parents have seen it on every other school site this month.

Name what the picture cannot settle. The age in the frame. How large the group is. Whether the adult in the room is the class teacher or a visitor who came for the shoot. If the youngest children are on the ground floor because the building has a stair you will not pretend is easy, say that beside the picture. A limit stated early becomes part of the decision. A limit discovered on a tour becomes a reason to feel misled.

Google's people-first guidance asks whether a page shows first-hand knowledge, including the knowledge that comes from actually visiting a place. A homepage written from a strategy workshop often fails that test. A homepage written from a Tuesday in October, with the noise and the work visible, does not.

Keep the crest for the footer or the letterhead. It is a mark of the institution. It is not evidence about the day. Parents are choosing the day.

## A visit on the first screen

The action is to visit or inquire. The control belongs with the students, not under a film, a newsletter, and a row of partner logos. Offer the next open morning, or a tour request that asks only for the child's year and a way to reply. If you publish a term's dates, the button should lead to those dates, not to a general mailbox with no hint of when anyone visits.

A parent comparing three schools will finish the two that say when they can walk the corridor. They will drop the one that offers a manifesto and a "contact us" with no shape. Inquiry is right when a visit is not the next step: a waiting year, a relocation, a question about support you need to discuss before a tour. For a local family in the admissions window, the visit is the door. Do not make them write an essay to reach it.

Label the button with the act. "Visit" or "Ask about a visit" is clear. "Begin your journey" hides the verb. "Explore" is what people do when the school has not decided what it wants them to do. Read the label as if you are a parent on a phone outside another school's gate. If you would not say it at that gate, change it.

If places for a year are full, say so next to the button. A visit offer that quietly has nothing to visit for is how trust frays. The page can still show the day. It should not pretend the door is open.

## Why the small mission line fails

A mission statement set in small type under a large crest reassures the board. It uses words the board approved. It does not show a child. From a phone, it is often illegible, which is a kindness the layout did not intend. The parent was never going to make a years-long decision from "fostering lifelong learners in a nurturing community." Those words fit the other two schools on the list.

The line also delays the day. It occupies the first screen that should have been a classroom and a date. Nielsen's first 10 seconds get spent on a sentence nobody will quote at the dinner table. What gets quoted is "the six-year-olds were reading aloud, and the group was small enough to count."

If the mission is true, it will be visible in the day you photograph. A small reading group is a mission you can prove. The sentence can live on the about page, in normal type, under a name, for the parent who asks what you claim to value. It should not be the toll paid to see the students.

Cousins of the same failure: a slow animation of the shield, a drone shot of the roof, a black frame with a Latin motto, an empty chapel with cinematic light and no one in it. Each treats the homepage as a ceremony. The parent is using it as a comparison.

Put the motto on the prospectus cover if the board requires a cover. On the site, let the Tuesday go first.

## What comes after the first screen

After the day and the visit, add only facts that change a choice. Four or five is enough.

- The ages you teach, in numbers, and the year a child would enter.
- The shape of the day in hours: start, lunch, end, and whether after-school care exists and until when.
- Who is responsible for the class. "A class teacher who stays with the group" is a fact. "Dedicated staff" is not.
- One limit: no bus route, a stair, a uniform that is specific, a waiting list for a named year, a faith expectation if you have one and it is real.
- A link to fees, for the parent who will not book a visit until they know the shape of the cost.

Stop before a slider of crests, a news grid from three years ago, and a quote from a parent with no context. If a line would not be said at the gate, it does not belong above the footer.

The heading should name the school and the ages. "Welcome" names nothing. A parent with two other tabs should know, from the heading and the first picture, which school this is and roughly how old the children in the picture are.

A map earns its place when it teaches the trip. "A twelve-minute walk from the station, with no parking on the street" is a fact. A pin on a city is furniture.

## Crest, lawn, and the empty room

Leave the history of the foundation, the list of notable alumni, and the building's architectural tour on inner pages. They can matter to a parent who already loves the day. They are a poor toll booth.

Skip an icon row labeled academic, pastoral, and co-curricular. Those categories are how a prospectus is printed. They are not how a parent pictures Thursday. Skip a popup that asks for an email before the visit dates are visible. Skip a photograph of a child you cannot identify as yours, shot from behind on a lawn that could be anywhere.

If a parent has said something useful, quote one sentence about the day, with permission, and keep the child unnamed or first-name only in the way your safeguarding practice already requires. A wall of stars is the wrong metaphor. You are not a product with ratings. You are a school. One true sentence is enough on the homepage. Longer proof belongs on its own page.

Policies that parents hunt for should be linked in plain words: admissions steps, fees, uniform, the visit. A homepage that pastes the policy book becomes a document. A homepage that hides the visit becomes a brochure.

## A pass you can do with someone who is not the board

Open the page on a phone, outdoors. Ask one question: on the first screen, can you see students in the day, and can you start a visit or an inquiry? If the answer is no, the page is in the wrong order. A sharper crest will not repair it.

Ask a parent who does not sit on your committees to say what a child does in the picture. If they say "stands near a logo," the picture failed. If they invent a facility you do not have, the picture misled them. Either result is a new frame, not a new tagline.

Read the first sentence aloud. Cut any line that could sit on the other two schools with the name swapped. What remains is the part only your Tuesday can say. The 10-second finding is not a plea to shout about excellence. It is a plea to be obvious about the day and the visit.

Do the pass after the last homepage meeting. A mission line restored "just in the header, very small" is the mistake returning by the side door. Freeze the first screen. Look again on a phone that is not yours.

## When the day is believable

Once a parent trusts the day, the next question is what the fees include and what they do not. That is a different page. [How to show the shape of the fees](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-an-independent-school) is the piece to read next, because a visit booked in ignorance of the cost wastes everyone's time, including the child's.

When you want that first screen argued from the parent's side, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring one photograph from a real Tuesday and the sentence the office says when a parent calls. That is enough to start.
